full_query:
A 26-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 6-month history of increasing lower back pain. He first felt the pain while lifting boxes at work but thought that he had just strained a muscle. The pain appears to be worse in the mornings and after rest. Exercise and physical activity appear to temporarily make the pain better. He has taken acetaminophen and ibuprofen for the pain. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. His temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 12/min. On physical exam, he is found to have limited flexion and extension of his spine as well as tenderness to palpation over the insertion of his patellar tendons bilaterally. Results from laboratory tests are shown below:

Serum:
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 61 mm/hr
C-reactive protein (CRP): 36 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L)

Which of the following is the most accurate test for this patient's condition? (A) Bone scan (B) Computed tomography (C) Magnetic resonance imaging (D) Radiograph (E) Ultrasound

shared_context.chief_complaint: increasing lower back pain for 6 months
shared_context.exam_findings: limited flexion and extension of spine, tenderness over insertion of patellar tendons

sentences: To determine the most accurate test for this patient's condition, let's analyze the provided information step-by-step
The patient's symptoms of increasing lower back pain that worsens in the mornings and after rest, and improves with exercise and physical activity, are characteristic of inflammatory back pain
However, the elevation in ESR and CRP levels (64 times and 3.6 times their normal values, respectively) also suggests an underlying inflammatory process

Given the presence of limited flexion and extension of the spine as well as tenderness to palpation over the insertion of the patellar tendons bilaterally, this is suggestive of spondyloarthritis (SpA), particularly ankylosing spondylitis
In spondyloarthritis, plain radiographs (X-rays) can show changes in the spine and sacroiliac joints, but they may not be visible in the early stages of the disease
Bone scans are not generally used for diagnosing spondyloarthritis; they are more often used for detecting bone metastasis or osteomyelitis

Computed tomography (CT) scans can provide more detailed images than X-rays and can help identify sacroiliitis and spinal changes in more detail, but MRI provides the most sensitive detection of early changes and is the preferred imaging modality for diagnosing spondyloarthritis
Ultrasound is not typically used for initial imaging of spondyloarthritis
Given the information, the most accurate test for this patient's condition is Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) since it provides the most sensitive detection of early changes in spondyloarthritis
